title: The Elegant Flirt 7
content:
Several disciples dug their poles into the water, dragging their spiritual nets in hot pursuit of that dark, darting silhouette. Shouts erupted from the other flank: “Over here, too!”

Another long shadow flickered under the surface. Half a dozen skiffs shot across the lake with nets trailing wide, but dredged up nothing but empty foam. Wei Wuxian’s brow pinched. “That’s bizarre. That shadow didn't look human at all. And it keeps warping—stretching, shrinking, shifting shapes… Lan Zhan, right by your hull!”

Bichen shot from the scabbard on Lan Wangji’s back, plunging like a strike of lightning into the lake. A second later, the blade whistled back into the open sky, dragging a crystalline rainbow of spray along its path. It hadn't nicked a thing.

Sword back in hand, Lan Wangji’s gaze chilled with intense gravity. Before he could speak, a junior disciple standing on a nearby boat flicked his wrist, sending his own blade flying into the deep after a shadow darting beneath his keel.

The moment that steel hit the water, it vanished. The disciple frantically pumped spiritual energy into his hand seals, chanting recalling mantras over and over, but the lake gave back nothing. It was as if the murky water had simply swallowed the blade whole. The boy looked about the same age as Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng; having lost his bonded sword, the color rapidly drained from his face. An older disciple standing near him chided, “Su She! We haven't even identified the threat—what possessed you to drive your sword into the deep on your own?”

Su She flinched, though he fought to keep his voice steady. “I saw the Second Young Master dispatch his blade, so I…”

The sentence trailed off as the boy realized how reckless and ignorant he sounded. Neither Lan Wangji nor Bichen were standards a common disciple could match. Lan Wangji could probe uncharted waters with his blade and pull it back untouched; ordinary cultivators enjoyed no such luxury. Humiliation flushed through Su She’s pale cheeks, burning with a touch of resentful shame as he stole a sideways glance at Lan Wangji. Lan Wangji didn't spare him a second look, his eyes glued to the dark current. In a flash, Bichen hissed out once more.

This time, the steel didn't dive. Instead, the tip skimmed the surface with surgical precision, hooking a darting shadow straight out of the water. A sodden, dripping clump of black fabric slapped wetly onto the deck. Wei Wuxian leaned on his toes to inspect it—it was just an old, rotted robe.

Wei Wuxian laughed so hard he nearly pitched headfirst into the lake. “Lan Zhan, you truly are a marvel! That’s a first for me—hunting water ghouls and fishing out their dirty laundry instead!”

Lan Wangji merely inspected the edge of his blade for grime, clearly having resolved to treat the nuisance like dead air. Jiang Cheng snapped, “Shut your trap! There wasn't a ghoul under that hull at all—it really was just a scrap of clothing!”

Wei Wuxian had clocked that too, of course; he just couldn't resist winding Lan Wangji up. “So the ghost slipping past our boats this whole time was just this rag? No wonder the nets slipped off and the swords couldn't pin it down—it keeps crumpling and shifting in the current. But a bunch of soggy silk can't swallow a cultivator's spiritual blade. There's definitely something else lurking down there.”

By now, the skiffs had drifted into the dead center of Lake Biling. The water here was extraordinarily dark, a heavy, suffocating shade of blackish-green. Suddenly, Lan Wangji’s chin lifted. “Turn back. Now.”

Lan Xichen asked, “Why?”

“Whatever is in this water led us here on purpose,” Lan Wangji said flatly. “It lured the boats to the center.”

The words hadn't even cleared the air when the hull beneath their boots dropped like a stone.

Freezing water rushed over the gunwales. Looking down, Wei Wuxian realized the lake was no longer murky jade—it had turned jet-black. A monstrous whirlpool was spinning silently into existence beneath the fleet, dragging the dozen wooden skiffs along its swirling rim, pulling them deeper by the second like a colossal maw opening in the deep to swallow them whole!

The air rang with metallic chimes as dozens of swords slipped their scabbards, cultivators leaping into the air to mount their flying blades. Drifting up into the sky on his own sword, Wei Wuxian glanced down and spotted Su She. The boy’s skiff was already halfway under the churning water, the dark current lapping past his knees. Terrified out of his skull, he hadn't even let out a yell for help. Without a second thought, Wei Wuxian leaned down, hooked his hand around the boy’s wrist, and yanked upward.

Taking on the extra deadweight made his blade dip violently, though it continued to climb. But before they could clear the spray, an immense, terrifying drag yanked through Su She’s frame, nearly ripping Wei Wuxian clean off his footing!

Su She’s lower torso had been sucked straight into the mouth of the black vortex. The eddy was spinning with savage speed, dragging him down by inches as though something lurking in the pitch-black depths was clamping both hands around his ankles, wrenching him under. Jiang Cheng was hovering casually twenty yards up on his blade, Sandu; spotting the chaos below, he dove down in sheer frustration, shouting, “What the hell are you doing now?!”

The vacuum pulling from the depths of Lake Biling was turning monstrous. Wei Wuxian’s sword, Suibian, was built for blinding agility and speed, lacking the raw, brute ballast needed to fight a current like this; the immense drag hauled him back down until his boots were nearly skimming the surface. Balancing his core against the vibrating steel, he clamped both hands around Su She’s arm and yelled up, “Someone lend a hand! If you don't haul us up, I'm dropping him!”

Suddenly, the fabric at his nape pulled taut. Wei Wuxian felt himself hoisted effortlessly into the air. Craning his neck, he found Lan Wangji dangling him by the back of his collar with a single hand. Though Lan Wangji kept his cool gaze fixed entirely on the horizon, he was piloting a single sword while bearing the weight of three grown men—fighting against an eldritch drag from the abyss—yet his ascent remained rock-steady, rising smooth and uninterrupted. Hovering nearby, Jiang Cheng felt a cold prickle of respect: If I’d dove down to carry them on Sandu, there's no way I could've climbed this fast or this steady. And Lan Wangji is barely my age…

Dangling in mid-air, Wei Wuxian called out, “Lan Zhan, your sword’s got quite the horsepower, doesn't it? Much obliged! But hey, why grab me by the scruff? Can't you hold my hand instead? This collar is choking me to death. Look, I’ll reach out, just take my hand.”

Lan Wangji’s voice was clipped. “I do not touch others.”

“Come on, we go way back!” Wei Wuxian whined. “How am I still an 'other'?”

“We are not familiar.”

Wei Wuxian put on a tragic, wounded pout. “You're so cold…”

Jiang Cheng finally lost his mind, roaring down at him, “You're the one being ridiculous! Can you shut your mouth for two seconds while you're being dangled by your scruff in mid-air?!”

The party beat a swift retreat on their flying swords, landing safely on the rocky shores of Lake Biling. Lan Wangji released his grip, turned with effortless grace, and addressed his brother: “It is a Water Abyss.”

Lan Xichen gave a grave, troubled sigh. “Then this is treacherous indeed.”

The moment the name Water Abyss dropped, both Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng understood. The real horror haunting Lake Biling wasn't a swarm of drowned ghouls—it was the water itself.

When rivers or lakes are plagued by treacherous currents and chronic shipwrecks over decades, the accumulated resentment and countless drowned souls will eventually breathe life into the body of water itself. Like a spoiled, aristocratic lady who refuses to go without luxury, the water grows addicted to human flesh and cargo; if it isn't fed regular sacrifices, it stirs up storms to claim its own toll.

Yet the people of Caiyi Town practically lived on boats and swam like fish; drowning accidents were practically unheard of, meaning a Water Abyss could never have developed here naturally. For it to take root in Lake Biling, there was only one possibility: someone had driven it here from somewhere else.

Once a Water Abyss matured, the entire lake turned into an immortal monster that was virtually impossible to slay. The only way to cleanse it was to drain every drop, dredge up every drowned corpse and rotted wreck, and let the lakebed bake dry under the sun for years on end—a completely impossible feat. However, there was a selfish, malicious workaround to save your own backyard: herd the entity downstream into someone else’s waters and let them deal with the plague instead.

Lan Wangji looked up. “Which region was recently troubled by a Water Abyss?”

Lan Xichen raised a slender finger, pointing toward the sky.

He wasn't gesturing at the heavens; he was pointing at the sun. Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng traded a knowing glance, the answer clear as day: the Qishan Wen Sect.

Across the land, cultivation clans were scattered like stars in the sky. Yet towering above them all stood a solitary, untouchable behemoth: the Qishan Wen Sect.

The Wen Clan took the blazing sun as their emblem, boasting that their glory would "rival the sun's brilliance and share its lifespan." Their ancestral domain was so colossal it rivaled an entire imperial city, named Nightless Sky—also hailed as the Immortal Capital of the Nightless City. Rumor had it that darkness never fell within its walls. They were an unchallengeable titan; in numbers, raw power, territory, and ancestral relics, no other clan could hold a candle to them. Countless wandering cultivators considered serving as a guest disciple under the Wen banner the crowning achievement of their lives. Given their notorious arrogance, dumping a Water Abyss on Caiyi Town was classic Wen behavior.

Having tracked down the root of the evil, the party fell into a heavy, suffocating silence.

If the Wen Clan was behind this, lodging protests or demanding accountability was entirely useless. They would never admit to it, and they certainly wouldn't pay a copper in compensation.

A Lan disciple grumbled in bitter indignation, “Dumping a monstrosity like that right onto our doorstep will ruin Caiyi Town. If the Water Abyss expands and creeps into the canals, thousands of innocent people will be living on the back of a dormant beast every single day. It's outrageous…”

Saddled with a chronic disaster someone else had thrown over their fence, the Gusu Lan Sect was looking down the barrel of endless future headaches. Lan Xichen let out a weary sigh. “Enough. Let us return to the town.”

Hiring fresh skiffs at the ferry landing, they punted back toward the bustling heart of the canals.

Passing beneath an arched stone bridge, the boats slid into the residential waterways—and Wei Wuxian’s shameless streak flared right back up.

Tossing his bamboo pole aside, he propped a boot on the gunwale, leaning over the water to check his hair in the reflection. He looked completely untroubled, showing not a trace of having just survived an ambush by water ghouls or slipping out of a Water Abyss's jaws, and immediately began tossing playful winks at the girls along the banks: “Hey there, big sister! How much for a pound of loquats?”

He was young, bright-eyed, and undeniably handsome, carrying a radiant, effortless charm like fallen peach blossoms drifting along a spring stream. A boat maiden adjusted her bamboo sunhat, looking up with a sweet, musical laugh: “Handsome young master, I’ll give you one for free—how’s that sound?”

The local Wu dialect was sugary, soft, and melodic. Coming off her lips, the words felt sweet as syrup, brushing against the ear like fragrant honey. Wei Wuxian cupped his hands in mock courtesy. “If it’s a gift from an elder sister, I’d be honored!”

The maiden dipped her hand into a woven basket, lobbing a plump, golden loquat through the air. “Don’t be so modest—it's on the house just because you’re so pretty!”

The current was swift, the two skiffs brushing past each other in a flash. Wei Wuxian spun around, catching the fruit with a clean snap of his fingers, grinning back at her. “And you’re even prettier, big sister!”

While he was busy playing the charming rogue, Lan Wangji stood as straight as a board on his own boat, eyes fixed dead ahead in untouchable, stony dignity. Wei Wuxian tossed the fruit into the air, caught it with a smirk, and suddenly pointed across the water. “Sisters! Take a look at him—isn't he handsome?”

Lan Wangji hadn't expected to get dragged into the clown show; before he could even muster a glare, the women along the canal chorused in unison: “Even prettier!” Somewhere in the crowd, a few boatmen even chimed in with hearty chuckles.

Wei Wuxian called out, “Then won't someone toss him one too? If you only give me one and leave him out, he’s going to get terribly jealous when we get back!”

A wave of musical giggles rippled down the waterway. Another maiden punting past called out, “Alright, alright, take two! Here, young master, catch!”

A second golden loquat landed securely in his palm. Wei Wuxian hollered over his shoulder, “Big sister, you're as sweet as you are gorgeous! Next time I'm in town, I’m buying a whole basket from you!”

The girl had a bolder streak, pointing straight at Lan Wangji as she laughed, “Bring him along too! Come buy them together!”

Wei Wuxian held the second loquat right under Lan Wangji’s nose. Keeping his gaze dead ahead, Lan Wangji snapped, “Move it.”

Wei Wuxian pulled it back with a theatrical shrug. “Figured you’d say that, which is why I had zero intention of handing it over anyway. Jiang Cheng, heads up!”

Jiang Cheng’s skiff skimmed past right on cue. Snatching the fruit out of the air with one hand, a brief grin broke across his face before souring into his usual scowl. “Still strutting your feathers, are you?”

Brimming with smug triumph, Wei Wuxian shot back, “Bite me!” Turning back to Lan Wangji, he pressed, “Hey, Lan Zhan, you grew up in Gusu, so you must speak the local dialect, right? Teach me a few words—how do people cuss in Gusu?”

Lan Wangji tossed him a cold “Ridiculous,” and stepped onto another boat. Wei Wuxian hadn't actually expected an answer anyway; the sugary, lilted dialect was just too amusing, and the thought of Lan Wangji speaking with that sweet cadence as a toddler was pure comedy. Tipping his head back, he took a swig of sweet rice wine from the glossy, pitch-black jug, scooped up his bamboo pole, and charged his boat forward to splash Jiang Cheng.

Over on their boat, Lan Wangji stood shoulder to shoulder with Lan Xichen. For once, the two brothers wore matching expressions—heavy-hearted, deep in thought as they turned over the logistics of containing the Water Abyss and delivering the grim news to the town magistrate.

A heavily laden cargo barge brushed past their port side, stacked to the brim with woven crates brimming with ripe, golden loquats. Lan Wangji’s eyes lingered on the fruit for a fraction of a second before snapping back to the horizon.

Beside him, Lan Xichen spoke up quietly: “If you'd like some loquats, shall we buy a basket to take back?”

Lan Wangji froze.

Flicking his sleeves in stony denial, he turned on his heel. “I do not!”

And with that, he marched off to find another boat.
